subject: Copywriting
title: Shirley Polykoff: Does She or Doesn't She?
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Shirley Polykoff: Does She or Doesn't She?.

hook.text: 'Does she or doesn't she? Only her hairdresser knows for sure.' Shirley Polykoff made hair dye respectable.

buildup.text: In 1956, only 7% of American women dyed their hair. It was considered scandalous—only 'certain women' colored.

discovery.text: Polykoff's Clairol campaign showed wholesome women and children. The message: dyed hair is natural, not shameful.

twist.text: Within six years, 70% of women were coloring their hair. One campaign transformed an entire cultural stigma.

climax.text: Polykoff showed that copy can change social norms, not just sell products. Her words rewrote what was acceptable.

punchline.text: From 7% to 70%. One copywriter erased a stigma.

quiz.question: What percentage of women colored their hair after Polykoff's campaign?

details.summary: Shirley Polykoff created 'Does She or Doesn't She?' for Clairol hair color in 1956, a double-entendre tagline that helped remove the stigma of hair dyeing. Within six years, the percentage of American women coloring their hair rose from 7% to over 50%, driven by Polykoff's brilliant...
details.whyItMatters: Polykoff showed that great copy can change social norms, not just sell products. Her work proved that addressing taboos with wit and discretion could unlock enormous untapped markets.
takeaways: The slogan made hair coloring socially acceptable for mainstream women
Hair dye usage jumped from 7% to over 50% during the campaign's run
The double meaning added playfulness that defused a sensitive topic

faq.question: Why was 'Does She or Doesn't She?' so effective?
faq.answer: The double meaning — does she dye her hair / is she that type of woman — made the taboo topic feel playful rather than shameful. The subtext was: if you can't tell, there's nothing wrong with it. It gave women permission to color their hair without judgment.

faq.question: How did the campaign change American culture?
faq.answer: Before Clairol's campaign, dyeing hair was associated with actresses and women of questionable reputation. Polykoff's ads featured wholesome mothers with children, normalizing the practice. By 1962, half of American women colored their hair — a complete cultural transformation.
